tldr: To help robots succeed even when stopping slightly off-target, this paper introduces a method that separately reconstructs the background and moving objects in 3D using navigation and manipulation camera feeds, synthesizing entire manipulation trajectories and action data from unseen robot base poses.
hero_caption: From demonstration trajectories collected at the original base pose (red and white robot), the framework synthesizes viewpoint images and end-effector actions from surrounding unseen base poses (yellow boxes). Because scenes with objects moving post-contact can be consistently re-rendered, the robot robustly executes tasks even under real-world base misplacements (blue boxes).
overview:
Visuomotor policies that control robot end-effectors directly from image inputs are easy to train using imitation learning. However, they suffer from a severe vulnerability: extreme sensitivity to subtle changes in camera viewpoint. This is especially problematic in mobile manipulation (MoMa), which combines a mobile base with a manipulator arm. Due to localization drift and obstacle avoidance constraints, it is nearly impossible to stop the base at the exact millimeter position used during demonstration collection. As a result, the camera view encountered during deployment diverges from training, causing policies to quickly break down.

Recently, researchers have tried augmenting training data by rendering novel-view synthesis (NVS) images from a few demonstrations. However, existing techniques assume static scenes. Consequently, they fail to correctly re-render moving objects during the critical post-contact interaction phase, leading to geometric inconsistencies.

To address this, the authors focused on the standard MoMa data collection workflow itself. During navigation toward a workspace, the robot naturally observes the static environment from multiple angles; during the subsequent manipulation phase, it observes the moving target object up close. This work, "MoMaSplat," independently reconstructs the static background and the dynamic object from these two data sources using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and a 3D foundation model. It then synthesizes the scene, object, and robot arm from unseen base poses, remapping them into geometrically consistent end-effector actions.

Evaluated on five real-world tasks involving rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, as well as in simulation, MoMaSplat achieved an average success rate of 37% at unseen base poses—more than double the strongest baseline (17%). Furthermore, it demonstrated remarkable robustness by successfully completing tasks even with large base displacements of 30 to 40 cm, where all baselines completely failed.
contributions: Proposed a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework that synthesizes complete manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic post-contact object interactions.

Established an end-to-end pipeline leveraging navigation and manipulation logs to separately reconstruct static scenes and dynamic objects in 3D, geometrically retargeting end-effector actions and proprioceptive states.

Substantially improved robustness against unseen base stopping poses across five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving rigid and articulated objects, demonstrating high task success rates even under large displacements where prior methods fail.

sections.heading: Why is mobile manipulation so vulnerable to viewpoint shifts?
sections.summary: Visual imitation learning is highly fragile to camera viewpoint shifts. For mobile robots, navigation errors cause them to stop at different locations every time, creating a fatal issue. Existing novel-view synthesis augmentations assume static scenes and cannot augment the post-contact phase where objects move. This paper proposes combining wide-angle navigation views with close-up manipulation views to reconstruct dynamic objects in 3D, synthesizing full demonstrations from unseen base poses.
sections.details:
Visuomotor policies that predict robot joint or end-effector displacements directly from images are powerful, but they heavily depend on the narrow camera viewpoint distribution seen during training. In tabletop manipulation, the robot base is fixed. For mobile manipulators, however, this is not the case. No matter how accurately a robot follows a path, navigation uncertainty, wheel slippage, and obstacle avoidance cause slight variations in the base pose and orientation relative to the workspace every run.

Collecting massive teleoperated demonstrations across every possible base pose to overcome these viewpoint shifts is practically infeasible. This has turned attention toward novel-view synthesis (NVS) techniques using NeRF or 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to virtually generate unseen viewpoints.

However, existing NVS approaches have a critical blind spot: they assume the entire scene is static. Consequently, they cannot correctly render moving objects during contact interactions, such as grasping and lifting. This limits data augmentation strictly to pre-contact reaching motions, leaving post-contact trajectories—the most delicate phase—completely unaugmented.

MoMaSplat elegantly solves this dilemma. Demonstration data from mobile robots naturally contains two phases: an approach sequence toward the workspace (where the static background is seen from diverse angles) and an actual manipulation sequence (capturing the moving object up close). By cleverly bridging these two streams, MoMaSplat independently models the static background and dynamic objects in 3D, automatically generating complete manipulation demonstrations from arbitrary base poses.

sections.heading: How does it fundamentally differ from simulation and conventional image augmentation?
sections.summary: This section reviews three related areas: simulation-based trajectory generation, real-image data augmentation, and base placement in mobile manipulation. It highlights real-world rollout costs, sim-to-real gaps, and static scene assumptions in prior work, clarifying the advantages of this method in handling dynamic objects directly from real capture data.
sections.details:
### Demonstration Synthesis via Simulation
Approaches that generate diverse viewpoints or randomized placements in simulators (such as X-Gen or MoMaGen) are actively studied. However, while motion plans generated by physics simulation are kinematically sound, they often require real-world rollouts to verify actual contact and dynamics, or they suffer from severe sim-to-real gaps. MoMaSplat directly reconstructs scenes and objects from real video feeds, avoiding reliance on physics engine modeling errors.

### Data Augmentation from Real Captures
Frame-level 2D augmentations or video generation models used as neural simulators often introduce geometric inconsistencies and hallucinations. In contrast, methods using 3DGS or ZeroNVS (such as VISTA) maintain geometric consistency, but they are restricted to static scenes or pre-contact reaching motions. By explicitly separating and integrating the static background and dynamic objects, MoMaSplat maintains consistency across the entire trajectory, including contact phases.

### Mobile Manipulation (MoMa)
Prior studies have used Inverse Reachability Maps (IRM) to geometrically determine base parking spots, or optimized test-time poses to match training viewpoints (such as Mobi-$\pi$). However, these require pre-scanning environments or running complex test-time optimization. MoMaSplat takes the opposite approach by instilling broad base-pose robustness directly into the policy, fundamentally easing precision demands on base positioning during deployment.

sections.heading: Separating backgrounds and moving objects into 3D to synthesize novel views and actions
sections.summary: The method reconstructs the static background from navigation logs and dynamic objects from manipulation logs, aligning their coordinate frames via navigation camera trajectories. From sampled unseen base poses, it renders the background, object, and arm, blending them with alpha compositing and retargeting end-effector actions and proprioception to mass-produce consistent novel demonstrations.
sections.details:
### III-A 3D Reconstruction
The environment is decomposed into three elements: static background, dynamic object, and robot body.
- **Static Scene Reconstruction**: Using RGB frames from the navigation trajectory $\mathcal{D}_{\text{nav}}$, COLMAP estimates camera poses and a sparse point cloud to build a 3DGS model. To handle transient artifacts across demonstrations, WildGaussians uncertainty modeling is incorporated. Segmentation masks remove the object and robot, preventing "ghosting" artifacts of the static object on the background. Absolute metric scale is recovered using the median ratio of onboard depth sensor measurements.
- **Dynamic Object Reconstruction and Coordinate Alignment**: Because the target object moves during manipulation, FastVGGT (a feed-forward 3D foundation model that estimates camera poses from unposed RGB sequences) is applied to background- and robot-masked frames, yielding object-centric camera poses. Since these estimates lie in an arbitrary coordinate system with unknown scale, the method uses navigation frames where the object is still static as a bridge. Using the correspondence between SfM and foundation model camera trajectories during navigation, Umeyama's algorithm solves for a similarity transform $\mathbf{S} \in \mathrm{Sim}(3)$ in closed form to align them into the world frame. Object 3DGS parameters and poses are then jointly optimized by minimizing photometric error.

### III-B Synthesizing Demonstrations from Unseen Base Poses
- **Base Pose Sampling**: New base positions are sampled within a $1.2 \times 1.2$ m region around the original base pose, with base yaw oriented to keep the target object centered in view. Arm reachability (IK solvability) is verified across multiple timesteps; unreachable poses are discarded.
- **Novel-View Rendering and Depth Compositing**: From the new viewpoint, the framework renders the background $\mathcal{G}_{\text{scene}}$, object 3DGS $\mathcal{G}_{\text{obj}}$, and the robot arm reproduced from joint angles in simulation (OmniGibson). The resulting three RGB, depth, and alpha maps are depth-sorted from near to far and composited using pixel-wise alpha blending, producing synthetic images with accurate occlusions.
- **Action and Proprioception Retargeting**: Changing base poses requires transforming end-effector actions $a_t = (p_t, o_t, g_t)$ (translational delta, rotational delta, gripper state) and end-effector poses defined in the base frame. Using the geometric transformation between base frames $\Delta^i_j T$, translation deltas are rotated and axis-angle rotation deltas have their axes transformed, generating correct action labels that trace the exact same world-frame end-effector path.

### III-C Imitation Learning
A visuomotor policy is trained with Diffusion Policy, sampling from original demonstrations $\mathcal{D}_{\text{src}}$ and synthesized data $\mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}}$ at a 1:3 ratio (25% and 75%).

captions.F2: The overall MoMaSplat pipeline. Navigation and manipulation feeds are decoupled to build 3DGS models of the static scene and dynamic object, which are unified into a shared coordinate frame via a Sim(3) transformation (left). Next, background, object, and robot arm are rendered from newly sampled base poses into composited images, and action labels are retargeted based on geometric transformations for policy training (right).

sections.heading: Validated on five real-world tasks: remarkable robustness despite large base misplacements
sections.summary: Evaluations across three real-world rooms, five tasks (rigid and 1-DoF articulated objects), and simulation confirmed high performance. At unseen base placements up to 40 cm away where existing augmentations completely collapsed, MoMaSplat maintained an average success rate of 37% (over double the strongest baseline), showing high visual and geometric fidelity.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Five manipulation tasks were designed across three real-world scenes:
- Desk environment: (i) pick-and-place bottle, (ii) open drawer
- Living room environment: (iii) pick-and-place remote, (iv) close laptop
- Kitchen environment: (v) open air fryer basket
These cover both rigid bodies and articulated objects (such as laptops and drawers), modeling only the moving link as a dynamic object. Four baselines were evaluated: "Source Only" (no augmentation), "Action Augmentation" (adding noise to end-effector states and actions), "VISTA" (changing viewpoints without transforming actions), and "One-Thousand Trajectories" (a 3DGS baseline modeling only backgrounds, combined with this paper's action transformation). Policies were rolled out at 12 unseen base poses per task with 3 trials each (36 evaluations per task).

### IV-B Results and Analysis
- **Performance at Unseen Base Poses**: While all methods performed similarly at the original demonstration pose, results diverged dramatically at unseen poses. Average success across all five tasks collapsed for Source Only (6%), Action Augmentation (6%), and VISTA (8%), while One-Thousand Trajectories (scene-only 3DGS) reached 17%. In contrast, MoMaSplat achieved 37%, more than doubling the strongest baseline.
- **Displacement Tolerance**: The gap widened as the base moved further away. Past 10 cm, baselines dropped to nearly 0% success. MoMaSplat maintained 33% success at 30 cm displacement on bottle pick-and-place, and 50% at 40 cm displacement on laptop closing.
- **Demonstration Efficiency**: In ablation experiments varying demonstration counts (10, 50, and 90 demos), MoMaSplat-augmented policies maintained 33%, 42%, and 50% success rates at unseen poses displaced by 10 to 20 cm. Without augmentation, using 90 demos yielded only an 8% success rate, demonstrating the critical value of data augmentation.
- **Fidelity Validation**: Compared against simulation ground truth, MoMaSplat achieved PSNRs of 26.40 dB on static scenes and 18.18 dB on dynamic objects, tracking object position and orientation with average errors of only $1.46$ cm and $4.01^{\circ}$.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future work: modeling contact dynamics and unobserved occlusions
sections.summary: MoMaSplat mitigates base stopping errors in visual imitation learning by synthesizing full trajectories including dynamic interactions from novel viewpoints. However, the authors also address limitations, including the lack of contact force simulation and challenges in reconstructing background regions initially hidden behind objects.
sections.details:
### Conclusion
By exploiting data collection workflows unique to mobile manipulation, this work decomposes static backgrounds and dynamic objects into 3DGS representations, achieving high-quality novel-view demonstration synthesis that includes contact interactions. Across diverse real-world tasks, it demonstrated extraordinary robustness against base pose uncertainties during deployment.

### Limitations and Future Work
- **Missing Occluded Regions**: Because the background model $\mathcal{G}_{\text{scene}}$ is constructed from pre-interaction navigation video, regions hidden at the start—such as the desk surface beneath a bottle, or the inside of a closed drawer or air fryer—are not observed beforehand. Once an object is lifted or opened, these newly revealed surfaces cannot be reconstructed, leaving visual artifacts during rendering.
- **Unmodeled Contact Dynamics and Physics**: The method performs geometric trajectory transformation and replay without simulating contact forces or object dynamics. Its applicability is limited in tasks where friction or reactive forces significantly alter execution.
- **Object Assumptions**: The framework primarily targets rigid bodies and 1-DoF articulated objects. Handling deformable items like cloth or ropes, severe occlusions, or featureless textureless objects remains an open challenge.

takeaways: A clever design principle: utilizing the natural separation in MoMa data collection—navigation logs for backgrounds and manipulation logs for dynamic objects—to construct unified 3D representations.
In visual imitation learning, simply perturbing actions or states fails to address base displacement; geometrically correct view synthesis paired with action retargeting is essential.
Augmenting complete trajectories including dynamic interactions enables robots to complete tasks 30 to 40 cm away from demonstrated poses, greatly easing precision requirements on navigation.
limitations: Cannot reconstruct initially hidden regions (e.g., table surfaces under objects or inside closed drawers) because background models are built only from pre-interaction navigation views.
Does not simulate physical contact forces or dynamics, relying solely on geometric trajectory following, which risks failure under heavy physical resistance.
High-fidelity 3DGS reconstruction remains difficult for deformable objects, textureless items, or environments with severe camera occlusions.
